title: Covenant at Shechem: Choose Whom You Will Serve
summary: Joshua gathers all Israel at Shechem and retells their history as the LORD's own story, from Abraham's idol-worshiping family to the gift of the land. He calls them to put away other gods and serve the LORD, declaring that he and his household will do so. The people pledge themselves three times, Joshua makes a covenant with them and sets up a stone as witness, and the book closes with three burials: Joshua, the bones of Joseph, and Eleazar the priest.
story: This is the end of the book of Joshua and the end of an era. The promise made to Abraham in Genesis 12, that his descendants would receive the land, has been fulfilled; now the question is whether they will serve the God who gave it. The previous chapter was Joshua's warning to the leaders; this one is a covenant ceremony for the whole nation. The burial of Joseph's bones closes a thread that runs back to Genesis 50, where Joseph asked that his bones be carried up from Egypt. The notice that Israel served the LORD through the lifetime of Joshua and the elders who outlived him (verse 31) prepares for Judges, which begins by telling what happened when that generation was gone.
historical:
Shechem lay in the hill country between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, near modern Nablus, at a natural crossroads. It was an old and sacred site in Israel's memory. Abraham built his first altar in the land there (Genesis 12:6-7). Jacob bought land there from the sons of Hamor (Genesis 33:19), and there Jacob's household buried their foreign gods under the oak (Genesis 35:4). Joshua had already led a covenant reading between Ebal and Gerizim (Joshua 8:30-35). Excavations at Tell Balata, the site of ancient Shechem, have uncovered a large fortified city from the Middle and Late Bronze Ages, including a large temple building, which confirms Shechem's importance in this period.

The historical review names real places and powers: Terah's family beyond the Euphrates (Ur and Haran in Mesopotamia), Esau's territory at Mount Seir in Edom, the Amorite kingdoms east of the Jordan under Sihon and Og, and Balak king of Moab, who hired the seer Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22 to 24). Joshua died at 110, the same age as Joseph (Genesis 50:26), a number Egyptian texts also used for an ideal full life. He was buried at Timnath-serah, the town given to him in 19:50.
cultural:
Since the 1950s many scholars, following George Mendenhall and others, have compared this chapter with treaties between great kings and their vassals from the ancient Near East, especially Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC. Those treaties typically named the great king, recited his past kindnesses to the vassal, laid down obligations of loyalty, called witnesses, provided for the document to be deposited and read, and listed blessings and curses. Joshua 24 has several of these features: a history of what the LORD has done, the demand for exclusive loyalty, witnesses (the people and a stone), and a written record. Scholars debate how close the match is and what it says about the chapter's date, but the comparison helps a modern reader see that Israel understood its relationship with God as a covenant with a king.

Setting up a large stone as a witness was a familiar practice. Jacob and Laban did the same at Galeed (Genesis 31:44-52). The stone stands under the oak near the sanctuary, a sacred tree at a holy place. The mention of household gods from beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt (verse 14) is striking: it admits that some Israelites still kept such images. Worship of more than one god was the normal assumption of the ancient world, and exclusive loyalty to one God was the unusual demand.
literary: The chapter is built as a covenant ceremony. Verses 2 to 13 are a prophetic speech in which the LORD speaks in the first person (“I took,” “I gave,” “I sent,” “I brought”), and the word I dominates. Israel's history is told as God's action from start to finish; even the victories were not won by your own sword or bow (verse 12). Then comes the choice. Joshua's challenge in verse 15 is sharpened by irony: if serving the LORD seems wrong, choose which gods to serve, the old ones of Mesopotamia or the local ones of Canaan. The dialogue that follows goes back and forth three times, with the people's pledge growing firmer and Joshua pushing back, most startlingly in verse 19. The key word is serve (the Hebrew avad), repeated more than a dozen times. The chapter, and the book, ends with three graves, marking the passing of the generation that entered the land.

outline.t: The LORD's story: from Terah to the land
Joshua's challenge: choose whom you will serve
The people pledge, Joshua warns, the people pledge again
Covenant, written record, and stone of witness
Three burials: Joshua, Joseph's bones, Eleazar

doctrines.note: The chapter is a covenant renewal: God's gracious acts come first, and Israel's obligations answer them. Grace precedes demand, and the demand is exclusive loyalty.
Joshua's warning in verse 19 rests on who God is: holy and jealous, not a deity who can be added to a shelf of others. His jealousy is the exclusive love of a covenant partner, not petty envy.

The history in verses 2 to 13 reads every event, from Abraham's call to Balaam's blessing to the hornet, as the LORD's doing. Israel owns land it did not work and cities it did not build because God gave them.

Joshua's call to put away the gods of the fathers admits that idolatry was not only a Canaanite temptation but part of Israel's own past and present. Serving God means actively removing rivals, not only adding him.

words.note: Avad, to serve. The word covers the work of a slave, the service of a vassal to a king, and the worship of a god. Its heavy repetition in this chapter makes the point that everyone serves something; the only question is whom. Israel, freed from serving Pharaoh, is called to serve the LORD.

Bachar, to choose. It is often used of God choosing Israel. Here, unusually, Israel is invited to choose. Joshua's challenge doesn't imply that God's choice waits on theirs; it calls them to answer his choice with their own.

Qanno, jealous, a word used only of God in the Old Testament. It describes his zeal for an exclusive relationship, like a husband's rightful claim on his wife's faithfulness. It is closely tied to the ban on other gods in the Ten Commandments.

Even, stone. The great stone set up under the oak becomes a witness that has heard all the LORD's words (verse 27). Stones in this book mark memory: the twelve stones from the Jordan (chapter 4), the heap over Achan, and now this one.

christ: Joshua's name is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus, and Hebrews draws the link directly: Joshua led Israel into the land, but he did not give them the final rest, which remains for God's people (Hebrews 4:8-9). This chapter shows why. Israel's pledge was sincere and short-lived. Joshua's warning that they were not able to serve the LORD proved true in the book of Judges. The New Testament presents a new covenant, promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34, in which God writes his law on the heart, established through Christ's blood (Luke 22:20). The pattern here, God's saving acts first and then the call to wholehearted service, is also the pattern of the gospel. The connection is thematic and covenantal rather than a prediction.

hard.q: Why does Joshua tell the people they are not able to serve the LORD and that he will not forgive them?
hard.a: Verse 19 is startling after so much grace. Most interpreters read it as a deliberate shock meant to test the people's resolve: Joshua wants them to count the cost rather than make an easy promise. The phrase about not forgiving is set in context by verse 20: it warns against deliberate, persistent covenant-breaking by those who forsake the LORD for other gods, not against the sins that the sacrifices of the Law were given to cover. Some also see a sober realism in the words, since Joshua knows Israel's record, and the following book proves him right. Read in the whole canon, the verse shows a need that the covenant alone could not meet, which the prophets later address with promises of a new heart.

questions: Joshua tells Israel's history as God's story, with God as the one acting. How would you tell your own story if you told it that way?
Joshua says everyone serves something. What are the modern versions of the gods beyond the River and the gods of the Amorites?
Why do you think Joshua pushed back so hard when the people promised to serve the LORD? What makes a promise to God more than words?
